about: Fun facts bundled with Inkframe, written for the frame in our own words: only well-established facts, each with a category and a short source note (an institution or reference work). Fields: id, text, category, source.

facts.text: Water is densest at about 4 °C, which is why ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down rather than the bottom up.
Sound travels about four times faster through water than through air.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.
Helium was discovered in the spectrum of the Sun in 1868, decades before anyone found it on Earth.
A diamond and the graphite in a pencil are both pure carbon; they differ only in how the atoms are arranged.
Absolute zero, the lowest temperature possible, is −273.15 °C.
The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, because the metre is defined from it.
Old window panes are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because glass slowly flows.
A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C, roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Hydrogen is the lightest element and the most abundant one in the universe.
The air we breathe is about 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen; everything else fits in the last 1 %.
Table salt is made of sodium, a metal that bursts into flame in water, and chlorine, a poisonous gas.
Atoms are mostly empty space: if the nucleus were a marble, the whole atom would be the size of a football stadium.
Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet about one metre square.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the periodic table in 1869 and left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered.
Marie Curie is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics and chemistry.
A rainbow is always a full circle; from the ground we usually see only the top half of it.
The ozone layer sits mostly 15 to 35 km up and absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet light.
Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide; at −78.5 °C it turns straight from a solid into a gas without melting.
An electron weighs about 1,800 times less than a proton.
Radio waves, microwaves, visible light and X-rays are all the same thing: electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when a mould contaminated one of his bacterial cultures.
Water boils at a lower temperature the higher you climb; on the summit of Everest it boils at about 70 °C.
Sunlight is white; a prism splits it into colours because each wavelength bends by a slightly different amount.
Ice is slippery because a thin film of liquid water forms on its surface, even well below freezing.
Every magnet has two poles; cut one in half and each piece has a north and a south pole of its own.
Aluminium was once more precious than gold; Napoleon III reportedly served his most honoured guests on aluminium plates.
The metre was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator through Paris.
Hydrogen and oxygen both feed a fire, yet combined they make water, which puts one out.
The Celsius scale originally ran the other way: Anders Celsius set 0 as the boiling point of water and 100 as freezing.
A mole of anything contains about 602 sextillion particles, a number named after Amedeo Avogadro.
Sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space; there is nothing there for the waves to move through.
Carbon dating works because living things take in carbon-14 and stop when they die; half of it decays every 5,730 years.
Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic: each whole number step means about ten times more ground shaking.
Water is the only common substance found naturally as a solid, a liquid and a gas on Earth’s surface.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and named them X because he did not know what they were.
A day on Venus is longer than its year: the planet spins once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in 225.
Jupiter is so large that more than 1,300 Earths would fit inside it.
The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year.
A teaspoon of material from a neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
Saturn is less dense than water; it would float in a bathtub big enough to hold it.
The footprints the Apollo astronauts left on the Moon will last for millions of years; there is no wind or water to erase them.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the solar system, about two and a half times the height of Everest.
Light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, takes more than four years to reach us.
About a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
The Sun holds about 99.8 % of all the mass in the solar system.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere to hold heat, so its nights fall to around −180 °C after days of about 430 °C.
Uranus spins on its side, its axis tilted about 98 degrees, probably after a giant collision long ago.
A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years; in 2011 it completed its first orbit since its discovery in 1846.
Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for at least 150 years.
Astronomers estimate there are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth’s beaches.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew sees around 16 sunrises a day.
The Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy are on course to merge in about four billion years.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the International Astronomical Union.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object and has crossed into interstellar space.
The Moon has no atmosphere to scatter light, so its daytime sky is black.
Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide, ordinary rust.
The Sun and the Moon look the same size in our sky because the Sun is about 400 times wider and also about 400 times farther away.
Jupiter’s moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury.
Saturn’s rings are made mostly of water ice, in pieces from grains of dust to chunks the size of a house.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched on 4 October 1957 and circled Earth for three months before burning up.
Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space on 12 April 1961, orbiting Earth once in 108 minutes.
The Apollo 11 astronauts spent about two and a half hours walking on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
Venus, at around 465 °C, is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun, because its thick atmosphere traps heat.
A comet’s tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, whichever way the comet is moving.
Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years; it was last seen in 1986 and is due back in 2061.
Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet, spinning once in just under ten hours.
A day on Mars is only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits about 540 km above Earth.
The temperature at the core of the Sun is about 15 million °C.
A full Moon is about 400,000 times fainter than the Sun.
Bamboo is a grass, and some species can grow almost a metre in a single day.
Young sunflowers track the Sun across the sky each day; mature flower heads settle facing east.
Coast redwoods in California are the tallest living trees; the tallest stand more than 110 metres high.
Bristlecone pines in California are among the oldest living trees; some are more than 4,800 years old.
Raindrops are not tear-shaped: small ones are spheres and larger ones flatten out like a hamburger bun.
Snowflakes have six sides because of the way water molecules bond as they freeze.
A Venus flytrap can count: a trap snaps shut only after a trigger hair is touched twice within about 20 seconds.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
The largest living organism by area is a honey fungus in Oregon that spreads under roughly nine square kilometres of forest.
Deserts are defined by low rainfall, not heat, which makes Antarctica the largest desert on Earth.
Seismographs record about 500,000 earthquakes a year; around 100,000 of them are strong enough to be felt.
A typical fluffy cumulus cloud weighs around 500 tonnes, yet floats because its water is spread over a vast volume of air.
Earth’s inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
About 71 % of Earth’s surface is covered by water, and the oceans hold about 97 % of it.
The deepest point in the ocean, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, is nearly 11 km down.
A tree adds one growth ring a year, wide in good years and narrow in dry ones; reading them is called dendrochronology.
Giant sequoias have bark up to 60 cm thick, which shields them from forest fires.
Coral reefs cover less than 1 % of the ocean floor yet support about a quarter of all marine species.
The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, so salty that swimmers float without effort.
The Amazon carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that the world’s rivers pour into the oceans.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things and can be seen from space.
Tiny drifting plankton in the oceans produce at least half of the oxygen we breathe.
Thousands of years ago the Sahara was a land of lakes and grassland; rock paintings there show swimmers and cattle.
Peat bogs preserve bodies for thousands of years because they are cold, acidic and starved of oxygen.
The largest hailstone recorded in the United States fell in South Dakota in 2010 and measured 20 cm across.
Antarctica’s ice holds about 70 % of the world’s fresh water.
Parts of the Atacama Desert in Chile are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga, and some lichens grow less than a millimetre a year.
A date palm seed about 2,000 years old, found at Masada in Israel, was successfully sprouted in 2005.
Old Faithful in Yellowstone erupts roughly every 60 to 110 minutes, throwing water up to 55 metres into the air.
Earth has recycled the same water for billions of years; the water you drink today may once have been drunk by a dinosaur.
A large tree can release hundreds of litres of water a day into the air through tiny pores in its leaves called stomata.
Hurricanes spin anticlockwise north of the Equator and clockwise south of it, because of Earth’s rotation.
Count the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres.
An octopus has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.
A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
A blue whale’s heart weighs around 180 kg and can slow to two beats a minute during a deep dive.
Sea otters hold paws while they sleep so they do not drift apart.
A cheetah can go from standing still to 100 km/h in about three seconds, quicker than most sports cars.
Honeybees visit about two million flowers to make a single pound of honey.
Crows can recognise individual human faces and remember them for years.
A mantis shrimp punches so fast that the water around its club briefly boils.
Sharks are older than trees: the first sharks appeared about 450 million years ago, the first trees about 390 million.
Starfish have no brain and no blood; they pump seawater through their bodies instead.
An ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain.
Butterflies taste with their feet: sensors there tell them whether a leaf is a good place to lay eggs.
Owls cannot move their eyes, so they turn their heads as much as 270 degrees instead.
A polar bear’s skin is black and its fur is transparent; it only looks white.
Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.
Emperor penguin fathers balance a single egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter, fasting for about two months.
Tardigrades can survive being frozen, boiled, dried out and exposed to the vacuum of space.
A giraffe’s neck has the same number of bones as a human’s: seven.
Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, the longest migration of any animal.
Koala fingerprints are so similar to human ones that they could confuse a crime scene investigator.
The axolotl can regrow lost limbs, parts of its heart and even parts of its brain.
A chameleon’s tongue can be as long as its body and shoots out in a fraction of a second.
Goats have rectangular pupils, which give them a wide field of view to watch for predators.
Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings.
Bats are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight.
Crocodiles cannot stick out their tongues; the tongue is fixed to the floor of the mouth.
A hummingbird’s heart can beat more than 1,200 times a minute.
Horseshoe crabs have blue blood, which medicine uses to test vaccines for contamination.
Monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,800 km to the same forests in Mexico, though no single butterfly makes the round trip.
Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror, a sign of self-awareness they share with great apes and dolphins.
The bowhead whale can live for more than 200 years, longer than any other mammal.
Cats cannot taste sweetness; they lack a working gene for the sweet receptor.
Nearly all wild penguins live south of the Equator; only the Galápagos penguin ranges just into the Northern Hemisphere.
A woodpecker’s tongue is so long that it wraps around the back of its skull when drawn in.
A sloth can take up to a month to digest a single meal.
Ants have no lungs; they breathe through tiny holes along their bodies called spiracles.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire: teaching at Oxford began by 1096, and Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
The Great Wall of China cannot be seen from orbit with the naked eye; it is long but very narrow.
The shortest war on record, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted around 40 minutes.
The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896.
Johannes Gutenberg’s printing press, developed around 1450, let books be produced far faster; his Bible was finished by about 1455.
The Hundred Years’ War between England and France actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
The Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for only 20 years after the 1889 World’s Fair; its value as a radio antenna saved it.
The first photograph to show a person was taken in Paris in 1838; a man having his boots shined stood still long enough to appear.
The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carries the same decree in Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphs, which let scholars decode Egyptian writing.
Vikings reached North America around the year 1000, five centuries before Columbus; their camp at L’Anse aux Meadows is in Newfoundland.
Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215.
Pompeii was buried by Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 and lay largely forgotten until its rediscovery in the 18th century.
The Wright brothers’ first powered flight on 17 December 1903 lasted 12 seconds and covered 37 metres.
The Berlin Wall stood from August 1961 until 9 November 1989.
The four presidents on Mount Rushmore took 14 years to carve, from 1927 to 1941.
In 1752 Britain and its colonies skipped eleven days to adopt the Gregorian calendar: 2 September was followed by 14 September.
The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France dedicated in 1886, was the colour of a copper penny before it weathered to green.
Tutankhamun’s tomb was found almost intact by Howard Carter in 1922.
The first message sent over the ARPANET, the ancestor of the internet, in 1969 was meant to be “login”; the system crashed after “lo”.
The oldest known cave paintings, in Indonesia and Spain, are more than 40,000 years old.
Stonehenge was built in stages between about 3000 and 2000 BC; some of its stones came from Wales, over 200 km away.
The Titanic sank on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg; around 1,500 people died.
Julius Caesar introduced the leap year in 46 BC as part of his Julian calendar.
The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed more than 13,000 houses, yet the records list only a handful of deaths.
The Colosseum in Rome opened in AD 80 and could hold about 50,000 spectators.
Napoleon was not unusually short: at about 1.68 m he was average height for a Frenchman of his time.
Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic in 1932.
Chess originated in India around the 6th century as a game called chaturanga.
Paper was invented in China; the court official Cai Lun is credited with perfecting it around AD 105.
An estimated 600 million people watched the first Moon landing on television on 20 July 1969.
The Black Death killed somewhere between a third and a half of Europe’s population in the mid-14th century.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to tilt during construction in the 12th century because of soft ground; it took nearly 200 years to finish.
Alexander Graham Bell was granted the patent for the telephone in 1876.
The Panama Canal opened in 1914 and spares ships a voyage of roughly 13,000 km around South America.
The Terracotta Army, more than 8,000 life-size soldiers buried with China’s first emperor, was found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776, but most of the delegates signed it on 2 August.
Russia is so wide that it spans eleven time zones.
Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
Africa is the only continent that lies in all four hemispheres: both the Equator and the Prime Meridian cross it.
Istanbul straddles two continents; the Bosporus divides its European and Asian sides.
Australia is wider than the Moon: about 4,000 km from east to west, against the Moon’s diameter of 3,475 km.
The Nile and the Amazon are the two longest rivers; which is longer depends on where you decide each one begins.
Mount Everest stands 8,849 metres above sea level, by the 2020 survey agreed by Nepal and China.
Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake on Earth and holds about a fifth of the planet’s unfrozen fresh water.
The Pacific Ocean covers more area than all the land on Earth put together.
Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, about 0.44 square kilometres.
Alaska is the northernmost and westernmost US state, and because the Aleutians cross the 180th meridian, the easternmost too.
The Sahara is roughly the size of the United States.
The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest point on land, about 430 metres below sea level.
Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, roughly the size of Austria.
Because Earth bulges at the Equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther from the planet’s centre than Everest’s.
Point Nemo in the South Pacific is the spot farthest from land, about 2,700 km from the nearest shore.
Greenland is the largest island in the world; Australia is larger but counts as a continent.
The Andes are the longest mountain range on land, running more than 7,000 km down the west of South America.
Reno, Nevada lies farther west than Los Angeles.
More than half of the world’s population lives in Asia.
The lowest temperature ever recorded on Earth, −89.2 °C, was measured at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983.
The Great Lakes hold about a fifth of the world’s surface fresh water.
The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
Including its islands, Norway’s coastline runs to more than 100,000 km.
Chile is about 4,300 km long but on average only about 180 km wide.
The Prime Meridian runs through Greenwich in London; it was agreed as the world’s zero of longitude in 1884.
Bolivia and Paraguay are the only landlocked countries in the Americas.
Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City are each surrounded entirely by a single other country.
Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia, is the highest navigable lake in the world, at about 3,800 metres.
The Danube flows through ten countries, more than any other river.
The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water in the world, about the size of Japan.
Venice is built on more than 100 small islands linked by about 400 bridges.
La Paz in Bolivia is the highest seat of government in the world, at about 3,600 metres.
Only about a quarter of the Sahara is sand; most of it is rock and gravel.
On a Mercator map Greenland looks as large as Africa, yet Africa is about 14 times bigger.
Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, is a dormant volcano that rises nearly 5,900 metres above sea level.
The word “alphabet” comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.
The dot over the letters i and j is called a tittle.
“Strengths” is one of the longest common English words with only one vowel.
English borrowed “robot” from Czech; the word was coined in Karel Čapek’s 1920 play R.U.R.
“The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” uses every letter of the alphabet; such sentences are called pangrams.
“Goodbye” began as a contraction of “God be with ye”.
E is the most common letter in written English; Q and Z are the rarest.
The first recorded uses of many English words, including “lonely” and “swagger”, are in Shakespeare’s plays.
“Nice” once meant foolish or ignorant; it comes from the Latin nescius, not knowing.
Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers of any language; English has the most speakers overall.
The @ sign has homely names abroad: a snail in Italian, a monkey’s tail in Dutch, a little duck in Greek.
Papua New Guinea has more than 800 living languages, more than any other country.
The ampersand was once recited as the 27th letter of the alphabet; its name comes from “and per se and”.
“Uncopyrightable” is a fifteen-letter English word in which no letter appears twice.
“Muscle” comes from the Latin musculus, little mouse, because a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin.
Basque, spoken in the Pyrenees, is unrelated to any other known language.
Japanese uses different counting words depending on the shape of what is counted: long thin things, flat things, small animals.
“Salary” comes from the Latin salarium, a word linked to sal, salt, though exactly how is uncertain.
Hawaiian is written with just thirteen letters: five vowels, seven consonants and the glottal stop.
Icelanders can still read their medieval sagas because the language has changed so little in 800 years.
“Dord” appeared in a 1934 dictionary as a word meaning density; it was a mistake, a misreading of the entry “D or d”.
“Quarantine” comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, the forty days ships waited off Venice in times of plague.
Esperanto, created by L. L. Zamenhof in 1887, is the most widely spoken constructed language.
English names for farm animals come from Old English and the words for their meat from French: cow and beef, pig and pork, sheep and mutton.
J was the last letter added to the English alphabet; it was separated from I only in the 16th and 17th centuries.
A palindrome reads the same backwards and forwards: “racecar”, or “A man, a plan, a canal: Panama”.
American Sign Language is not a signed form of English; it is a language of its own and closer to French Sign Language.
“Avocado”, “chocolate” and “tomato” all come from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.
“OK” first appeared in print in Boston in 1839 as a jokey abbreviation of “oll korrect”.
Finnish has no grammatical gender and no future tense, but its nouns have about fifteen cases.
“Clue” comes from “clew”, a ball of thread, after the thread Theseus used to find his way out of the labyrinth.
Spanish opens a question with an inverted question mark, ¿, so the reader knows from the first word.
The ancient Greeks and Romans usually wrote without spaces between words.
Upper- and lower-case letters take their names from the printer’s type cases: capitals were kept in the upper case.
“Nightmare” has nothing to do with horses: a mare was an evil spirit believed to sit on sleepers’ chests.
A contronym is a word with two opposite meanings: “cleave” can mean to split apart or to cling together.
Zero as a number in its own right was developed in India; the astronomer Brahmagupta set out rules for it in 628.
A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros; the name was coined by a nine-year-old, the nephew of the mathematician Edward Kasner.
111,111,111 multiplied by itself gives 12,345,678,987,654,321.
Every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order.
There are infinitely many prime numbers; Euclid proved it around 300 BC.
Just 39 digits of pi are enough to work out the circumference of the observable universe to the width of an atom.
A deck of 52 cards can be arranged in roughly 8 followed by 67 zeros ways, far more than the number of atoms in the Earth.
In a room of just 23 people there is a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday.
1729 is the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two different ways: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed, and 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.
The Fibonacci numbers, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on, turn up in the spirals of sunflower seeds and pine cones.
A prime number has exactly two divisors, and 2 is the only even one.
The Babylonians counted in base 60, which is why an hour has 60 minutes and a circle 360 degrees.
Roman numerals have no symbol for zero; the Romans simply did not need one.
The equals sign was introduced in 1557 by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines because nothing could be more equal.
Fold a sheet of paper in half 42 times and, in theory, it would be thick enough to reach the Moon.
The numbers 1 to 100 add up to 5,050; Gauss is said to have found this as a schoolboy by pairing 1 with 100, 2 with 99 and so on.
A million seconds is about eleven and a half days; a billion seconds is nearly 32 years.
The ancient Egyptians wrote fractions almost entirely with a numerator of 1, so three quarters became one half plus one quarter.
“Forty” is the only number whose letters are in alphabetical order, and “one” the only one whose letters run in reverse.
A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors: 6 is 1 + 2 + 3, and 28 is 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14.
The decimal point is a fairly recent idea; John Napier popularised it in the early 1600s.
Pi Day is 14 March, written 3/14 in the American style; Albert Einstein was born on that day in 1879.
A baker’s dozen is 13: medieval bakers added a loaf to avoid penalties for selling underweight bread.
The infinity symbol, a sideways figure eight, was introduced by the mathematician John Wallis in 1655.
Century years are leap years only when divisible by 400: 1900 was not a leap year, but 2000 was.
If the digits of a number add up to a multiple of 9, the number itself is divisible by 9.
The chance of a fair coin landing heads ten times in a row is 1 in 1,024.
A Rubik’s Cube has about 43 quintillion possible positions, yet every one of them can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.
Four colours are enough to colour any map so that no two neighbouring regions match; the proof, in 1976, needed a computer.
In binary, which uses only 0 and 1, the number 255 is written 11111111.
Mathematicians prefer radians to degrees: a full turn is two pi, about 6.283.
In a group of 70 people the chance that two share a birthday is better than 99.9 %.
Trisecting an arbitrary angle with only a compass and straightedge is impossible; Pierre Wantzel proved it in 1837.
Many clock faces show four as IIII rather than IV.
Take any four-digit number with at least two different digits, sort its digits high and low, subtract, and repeat: you always reach 6174.
The ancient Greeks wrote numbers with letters: alpha stood for 1, beta for 2, and so on through the alphabet.
Honey never spoils; pots of still-edible honey have been found in ancient Egyptian tombs.
Carrots were originally purple or white; the orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands in the 17th century.
Peanuts are not nuts but legumes, related to peas and beans.
For most of its history chocolate was drunk, not eaten; the Maya and Aztecs made a bitter, frothy drink from cacao.
Cashews grow at the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple, and their shells contain an irritant related to poison ivy.
Botanically, a strawberry is not a berry, but a banana is.
Saffron is the most expensive spice by weight; each crocus flower yields just three threads, picked by hand.
The sandwich is named after John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, who reputedly ate meat between bread so he could keep playing cards.
Vanilla comes from the seed pods of an orchid; outside Mexico the flowers have to be pollinated by hand.
Tea is the most widely drunk beverage in the world after water.
Ketchup began in Asia as a fermented fish sauce; tomatoes were only added in the 19th century.
Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air.
The fortune cookie was invented in California, not China, in the early 20th century.
A pineapple takes about two years to grow, and in 18th-century Britain the fruit was so prized that it could be rented for a party.
Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit: nutmeg is the seed, mace the red lacy covering around it.
Popcorn pops because each kernel holds a drop of water that turns to steam and bursts the hard hull at about 180 °C.
Capsaicin, the compound that makes chillies hot, triggers the same nerve receptors that respond to heat.
Bananas are very slightly radioactive because of the potassium they contain.
Almonds are the seeds of a fruit related to peaches and plums.
The croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl and became a French staple only in the 19th century.
White chocolate contains no cocoa solids, only cocoa butter, sugar and milk.
Coffee beans are the seeds of a cherry-like fruit; roasting brings out their flavour.
Roquefort ripens in the limestone caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon and has been protected by French law since 1925.
Tomatoes were once feared to be poisonous in Europe because they belong to the nightshade family.
The potato and the sweet potato are not close relatives: the potato is a nightshade, the sweet potato a morning glory.
Black, green, white and oolong tea all come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis; only the processing differs.
Stone Age chewing gum has been found: lumps of birch-bark tar, thousands of years old, still carrying tooth marks.
Ancient Romans seasoned almost everything with garum, a sauce made from fermented fish.
Rice is the staple food of more than half of the world’s population.
Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes around 8,000 years ago and reached Europe in the 16th century.
Pizza Margherita is said to have been named in 1889 for Queen Margherita of Italy, its tomato, mozzarella and basil the colours of the flag.
Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree, dried until it curls into quills.
Lobster was once so plentiful in New England that it was fed to prisoners and servants.
An old egg floats in water because the air pocket inside it grows as the egg slowly loses moisture.
It takes about 40 litres of maple sap to make a single litre of maple syrup.
The wasabi served in most restaurants outside Japan is horseradish dyed green; real wasabi is hard to grow.
Ice cream cones became popular at the 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis.
